lines: Take {gift_item}. A little comfort on the road never hurts.
Here, {gift_item}. Keep it close when the night gets cold.
Good. {gift_item} suited {tested_villager} like the right dye on clean wool.
Then the pattern held. {tested_villager} liked {gift_item}.
Wrong color for that cloth. For {gift_subject}, try {alternative_gift}.
{gift_item} clashed? Bring {alternative_gift}; softer on the eyes and temper.

messages.text: Wrong pattern. Pick up {alternative_gift} and leave {gift_item} out of it.
You followed the thread into a knot. Use {alternative_gift} next.

openings.text: Mind the loom. What do you need?

closings.text: Back to turning wool into warmth, then.

pacify.text: Fine. I will smooth this wool down for now.
That does not cover the tear. Bring {emerald_cost} {emeralds}.
No. The flock still startles when you come near.

lines: Scattered sheep make the whole day longer than it needs to be.
Wolves near the pens change how everyone listens after dark.
Clean wool is quiet proof that somebody did the dull work well.
Warmth is easy to praise after someone else made it.
A good blanket is village peace you can fold.
Patterns are easier to see when you stop yanking the thread.
Clean wool feels ordinary until winter reminds you it is not.
A spilled dye pot once made half the village look festive by mistake.
One late evening, the whole loom jammed because I trusted a knot.

lines.text: Mind the loom. Threads tangle faster when people crowd them.
My jokes have loose threads. Pull gently.
That thought tangled itself before it reached the loom.
Do not pull at work you do not understand.

lines: I remember being lost from the flock. You brought me back to the fold.
My thoughts were all tangled wool. You helped card them straight.
Your face feels familiar, soft in one place and snagged in another.
I remember shivering, then warmth returning one thread at a time.

lines.text: I remember you through panic and wool-dark dreams. Keep your voice low.

lines: Thunder shook the loom so hard the flock pressed hard against the fence, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked wool, fences, and the flock after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the loom, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the fences twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have fences to set right.
I checked wool, fences, and dry grass for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the wool after.
The loom can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the loom, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the loom, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
During a raid, the loom can wait; who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the loom still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before wool, fences, and the flock. That is the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the loom and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the loom, I saw fear cross the square; then I saw courage get there first.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the loom first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the pen beyond the lantern and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the loom enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a length of wool between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the loom, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning dust from the wool.
I checked wool, fences, and the flock, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the loom, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a shepherd which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the loom, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
The loom can wait. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the loom found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the loom. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing snow off the fence rails and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the loom. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
